findings.where: Hero, the supporting paragraph under Mark's line (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The one sentence that says what Mark does never mentions law or legal advice. It says 'advise … on infrastructure' and ends on a phrase that repeats itself ('Public-Private Partnerships that work as true partnerships'). The only legal signal on the first screen is the small grey credential line beside the logo. The heading is an opinion, so this paragraph is the only place the page can say what he offers.
findings.who_objects: A development-bank official who has come looking for a legal advisor on a PPP law. The first screen tells them he works on infrastructure in general and makes them infer the legal side from 'Formerly Lead Lawyer'. The founder would object too: the brief asks that the page reflect law, PPP and advice to governments.

findings.where: Phone first screen: the order of headline, address strip and supporting paragraph
findings.fault: On the phone the paragraph that says what he does and for whom comes after the yellow address strip, and falls below the first screen. A phone visitor gets the name, the photo, an opinion and an email address before learning what Mark offers or who it is for. Desktop puts the paragraph before the action, so the two widths tell the story in different orders.
findings.who_objects: An official opening the link on a phone, say from LinkedIn between meetings. The first screen does not answer 'is this for me?', and the contact action comes before they have a reason to use it.

findings.where: Contact route across the page: the nav (Profile, Articles, Blog), the article specimen, and the page end
findings.fault: The email address appears only in the hero strip. The nav has no Contact item, there is no footer carrying the address, and the article specimen shows no header, byline bio or address. So the design gives no way to reach Mark from a deep page or from the bottom of a long read.
findings.who_objects: An official who arrives on an article from a shared link, or who has scrolled past the hero. They have to go back to the homepage to find out how to write to him, and first-visit trust asks for the address on every page and a Contact label in the nav.

findings.where: Article specimen, the 'Download' block after the article's closing line
findings.fault: Under an article dated 18 September 2024 on 'The World's Best PPP Law', a bare 'Download' label offers a different piece: a 2026 lecture called 'Streamlining the PPP Process'. Nothing says it is a related or separate item. The link goes straight to a PDF, not to a page for the lecture.
findings.who_objects: A reader who expects 'Download' to give them this article as a PDF and gets an unrelated lecture. First-visit trust also asks for each publication on its own page, with the PDF behind it.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lectern photograph's grey grading (the treatment, not the stand-in photo)
findings.fault: The 'print in greys' grading turns the backdrop into a heavy near-black slab, the darkest mass on the light article page, and blows Mark's face out to chalky white. In colour on the hero he looks warm. In the article he looks harsh and archival, closer to a press-agency file photo than to 'real people in real light'.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Mark, since the brief asks for imagery graded into the house colours and real light, not stripped to stark monochrome. A reader also sees a cold, overexposed face of the person they are thinking of hiring.

findings.fault: This is a button (it acts here) dressed in the link's reserved treatment, blue with an underline. It looks like it goes somewhere, and every other blue underline on the page does go somewhere.
findings.who_objects: The founder judging the tile, and anyone who carries this control style into the site, where a blue underline must keep meaning 'link'.

findings.fault: The display title has a straight typewriter apostrophe, while the body, subhead and quotations use curly typographer's quotes. It shows most at display size.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader of legal and policy texts, for whom a straight quote in a set title looks unedited. It works against the 'legal journal' gravitas the direction claims.
